title: "False-positive rates that vary among sites and occasions"

  %\VignetteIndexEntry{False-positive rates that vary among sites and occasions}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# The fits below were run by dev/precompute-fp-variation.R and are read from
# fp-variation-results.rds, so that the article builds without Stan.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%")
library(crywolf)
res <- readRDS("fp-variation-results.rds")
est <- function(fit, var, digits = 2) {
  r <- fit$table[fit$table$variable == var, ]
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f [%.", digits, "f, %.", digits, "f]"),
          r$mean, r$lower, r$upper)
}
tab <- function(fits, vars) {
  out <- purrr::imap(fits, function(f, nm) {
    t <- f$table[f$table$variable %in% vars, c("variable", "mean", "lower", "upper", "rhat")]
    data.frame(model = nm, t)
  }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
  out[c("mean", "lower", "upper")] <- round(out[c("mean", "lower", "upper")], 3)
  out$rhat <- round(out$rhat, 3)
  out
}
```

```{r stale, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(crywolf:::.stale_note(res, "fp-variation-results.rds"))
```

The basic model has one false-positive rate for all sites and occasions,
or a rate that depends on site covariates through `fp = ~ ...`. Two other
patterns are common in acoustic data. The rate can differ among sites for
reasons nobody measured: a stream at one site, a frog chorus at another.
And it can change from one occasion to the next with conditions that are
measured on each recording, such as wind or rain noise. This article fits
both patterns to simulated data whose truth is known, and compares the
results with the constant-rate model.

The fitting code is shown but not run when the article is built; the
results come from `dev/precompute-fp-variation.R`.

## Unexplained variation among sites

### The model

With `random_fp = TRUE`, the logit of the false-positive rate of site $i$
gets a site effect,

$$
\mathrm{logit}(p_{10,i}) = \gamma_0 + \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\gamma} + e_i,
\qquad e_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{\mathrm{fp}}),
$$

where $\gamma_0$ is the intercept of the rate, $\mathbf{x}_i$ are the site
covariates of `fp` (none here), and $\sigma_{\mathrm{fp}}$, reported as
`sd_fp_site`, measures how much the rate varies among sites. Its prior is
half-Normal with scale `fp_priors()$fp_site_sd` (1 by default). Each site
effect is informed only by the automated detections of its own site, so with
few occasions per site the estimates are pulled towards the mean.

### The data

```{r among-data, eval = FALSE}
sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 200, nocc = 10, sigma_p10 = 1, frac_verified = 0.3,
                   seed = 1)
m_const <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE)
m_rand <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE,
                  random_fp = TRUE)
```

The rate of each site is drawn on the logit scale around a base rate of
`r res$among$truth$p10` with a standard deviation of
`r res$among$truth$sigma_p10`, which gives a mean rate over sites of
`r round(res$among$truth$p10_marginal, 3)`. The true occupancy slope is -0.8.

### Results

```{r among-table}
tab(list(constant = res$among$constant, random_fp = res$among$random),
    c("occ_x", "fp_(Intercept)", "p10_bar", "sd_fp_site"))
```

The constant-rate model estimates the occupancy slope at
`r est(res$among$constant, "occ_x")`, which misses the true value of -0.8.
With the site effect the estimate is
`r est(res$among$random, "occ_x")`, still below the truth but with an
interval that contains it, and the standard deviation of the site
effects, `r est(res$among$random, "sd_fp_site")`, covers the true value of 1.
Unexplained variation among sites is not harmless: in this dataset it pulled
the occupancy slope towards zero, as sites with a high false-positive rate
look occupied whatever their covariate. One dataset shows that it can
happen; `fp_calibrate()` with `sigma_p10` in the design measures how often.

`fp_sites()` gives the rate of each site, which with the site effect is a
compromise between the site's own data and the mean:

```{r among-sites, fig.cap = "False-positive rate of each site estimated with the site effect against the true rate used in the simulation, on log scales. The dashed line marks equality."}
s <- res$among$random$sites
s$truth <- res$among$truth$p10_site
ggplot2::ggplot(s, ggplot2::aes(truth, p10)) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "#241042") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "True false-positive rate", y = "Estimated rate (posterior mean)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

The estimates fall into two groups. The
`r sum(s$detections == 0)` sites without any automated detection all get a
low rate, between `r sprintf("%.3f", min(s$p10[s$detections == 0]))` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(s$p10[s$detections == 0]))`, whatever their true
rate; the sites with detections get higher rates, which track the truth
only loosely (correlation over all sites
`r round(cor(s$p10, s$truth), 2)`). Ten occasions per site say little about
one site's rate, and at a site that may be occupied a detection can be true
or false. The site effect matters for the occupancy slope through the sites
as a whole, not as a way to rank sites by their false-positive rate.

### Costs and caveats

* **Mixing.** The fit with the site effect took
  `r round(60 * res$among$random$minutes)` seconds against
  `r round(60 * res$among$constant$minutes)` for the constant rate, and its
  smallest bulk effective sample size was
  `r round(res$among$random$diagnostics$min_ess_bulk)` (largest R-hat
  `r round(res$among$random$diagnostics$max_rhat, 3)`). In 20 simulated
  datasets of the same kind with 300 sites and 20 occasions, 3 fits had an
  R-hat above 1.01 with the default
  settings (`dev/profile/rejected-2026-10-21.md`). Check the diagnostics, and
  run more iterations when they flag a problem.
* **Model comparison.** Leaving a site out means its own effect is not
  known, so `loo()` integrates each site's effect out of its
  log-likelihood (by Gauss-Hermite quadrature) before the leave-one-out
  computation. Conditional on the fitted effects, as in the `log_lik` of the
  Stan program, many sites would have Pareto $k$ above 0.7; integrated,
  `r sum(res$among$random$loo$diagnostics$pareto_k > 0.7)` do here. The
  difference in favour of the site effect is about
  `r round(abs(loo::loo_compare(list(constant = res$among$constant$loo, random_fp = res$among$random$loo))[2, "elpd_diff"] / loo::loo_compare(list(constant = res$among$constant$loo, random_fp = res$among$random$loo))[2, "se_diff"]), 1)`
  times its standard error, not a decisive one.

```{r among-loo}
loo::loo_compare(list(constant = res$among$constant$loo,
                      random_fp = res$among$random$loo))
```

* **Confounding.** The site effect is independent of the covariates by
  construction. It does not fix a false-positive rate that tracks the
  occupancy gradient: for that, model the rate on the covariates
  (`vignette("crywolf")`).

## Variation among occasions

### The model

A false-positive formula can use covariates of the automated table. The
rate then varies among the occasions of a site:

$$
\mathrm{logit}(p_{10,ik}) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\, \mathrm{noise}_{ik},
$$

where $\mathrm{noise}_{ik}$ is a measurement on occasion $k$ of site $i$,
standardized. The prior on $\gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}$ is the slope prior of
`fp_priors()`. Site and occasion covariates can be mixed in one formula.

### The data

The data were simulated with a background-noise covariate, drawn at random
for every occasion, that raises the logit of the false-positive rate by 1
per standard deviation, from a base rate of 0.05. In practice the covariate
is a column of the automated table:

```{r within-fit, eval = FALSE}
m_const <- fp_occu(d, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE)
m_noise <- fp_occu(d, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ noise, random_recorder = FALSE)
```

### Results

```{r within-table}
tab(list(constant = res$within$constant, noise = res$within$noise),
    c("occ_x", "fp_(Intercept)", "fp_noise", "p10_bar"))
```

The noise effect is estimated at `r est(res$within$noise, "fp_noise")`
(true value 1), and the mean rate over occasions at
`r est(res$within$noise, "p10_bar", 3)` (true value
`r round(res$within$truth[["p10_bar"]], 3)`). Because the noise was drawn
independently of the occupancy covariate, the constant-rate model still
estimates the occupancy slope well, at `r est(res$within$constant, "occ_x")`.
What it cannot do is say which detections are suspect: under the noise
model, a detection in a noisy recording counts as weaker evidence of
presence. LOO prefers the noise model clearly:

```{r within-loo}
loo::loo_compare(list(constant = res$within$constant$loo,
                      noise = res$within$noise$loo))
```

If noise were correlated with the occupancy covariate, as when noisy sites
are also those with less habitat, leaving it out would bias the slope as in
`vignette("calibration")`.

## Which to use

* A measured cause of false positives, at the site or the occasion level,
  belongs in the `fp` formula. It adds one coefficient per covariate rather
  than one effect per site, and modelling the measured cause is what
  restored calibrated intervals in the simulations of
  `vignette("calibration")` when the cause was correlated with occupancy.
* `random_fp = TRUE` is for variation among sites that no covariate
  explains. It costs time and mixing. It is off by default.
* With neither, the false-positive rate is assumed equal everywhere. A
  posterior predictive check (`fp_ppc()`) that flags sites with more
  detections than the model expects is a sign that this is wrong.
